claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: the signals come mostly from say fundamentals so you you look at things like fiscal monetary policy
claims.claim: Both discretionary and systematic macro use fundamentals (fiscal, monetary, growth, inflation) plus factors like value, mean reversion and carry; they differ in method.
claims.indicator: fiscal, monetary policy, growth, inflation, value, carry

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: multicolinearity in the world of machine learning doesn't really matter anymore because you can compress data
claims.claim: Quant macro can use many correlated inputs because machine learning compresses data, and uses nonlinear pattern-recognition regressions plus robust portfolio construction.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: if you try to do that I think you take a lot of alpha away from the program
claims.claim: A systematic program has to be rigid, since inserting news (a weekend AI release, tariff comments) manually removes alpha.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: our Quant programs typically run one to two month Horizon maybe three months
claims.claim: Graham quant macro runs on one to two (up to three) month horizons, while discretionary PMs trade week to week.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: to react and if you're a very good micro PM you're going to understand that as a as a potential Alpha signal right
claims.claim: A quant system does not react to a geopolitical accident, while a good discretionary macro PM treats it as an alpha signal, though the PM cannot process as much data as the quant.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: that I think is the the key advantage of the discretionary over every other strategy
claims.claim: The main advantage of discretionary macro is the ability to change view on the fly (big tariff, DeepSeek), which quant data processing cannot do.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: you can have the ability to make interventions that are not about Alpha ever but are about respons
claims.claim: Quant firms run a daily risk meeting to understand system positions; interventions in disruptions are risk responses, never alpha.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: machine learning the less you're going to be able to understand what things are doing
claims.claim: More big data and ML reduces interpretability, so humans must still understand how the system is trading.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: we don't like to use unsupervised machine learning I think it has a huge today it's super prone to over Feit so to perform incredibly
claims.claim: Unsupervised ML overfits (strong in sample, poor out of sample), so use ML for alpha discovery and then understand why the alpha exists.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: to discover Alpha then then we can converse and understand why that Alpha is there great Tool
claims.claim: AI is a great tool for discovering alpha, which humans then explain.

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: 25% is where we have discretionary PMS so we call that the discretionary fund a different way of dealing with the same problematics same markets same issues
claims.claim: Graham runs roughly 70-75% of its assets as quantitative macro and about 25% as discretionary PMs and treats the two as different methods applied to the same markets and the same problems, not as different businesses.
claims.indicator: share of assets in systematic vs discretionary

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: techniques like singular value composition data compression and pattern matching what have you they were there before cosign similarity but now we're using them in a cohesive way
claims.claim: Singular value decomposition, data compression, pattern matching and cosine similarity are old techniques; what is new is that AI now combines them into one coherent pipeline for extracting signals from large data.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: what drives macro performance and opportunities it's how much Central Bank movement there is
claims.claim: Macro opportunity set scales with the amount of central bank rate movement, because moves in policy rates drive FX and equity volatility.
claims.direction: more central bank movement = more FX/equity volatility = better macro opportunity
claims.testable: partly - could proxy opportunity by count of policy changes versus macro fund returns

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: in that 11-year period there were a total of 13 25 basis point equivalent hikes among all three
claims.claim: Data point: 2010-2021 saw only 13 25bp-equivalent hikes across ECB, BoE and Fed, versus 26 in 2022 alone with 44 priced for the year, explaining why macro was starved in the prior decade and rich now.
claims.testable: yes - count is checkable from policy rate histories

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: you have a very Divergent set of circumstances in Europe compared to the US compared to Japan and so on and so that's just good for macro Trading
claims.claim: Divergence in central bank policy across regions (Europe, US, Japan) creates relative-value and FX trades that favour macro trading.
claims.indicator: policy-rate divergence across major central banks
claims.direction: long dollar vs yen while BoJ holds its band
claims.testable: partly - divergence measure definable, link to returns needs testing

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: the dollar ends at 146 or something today uh you know if they were to release that band there'd be a lot of opportunity on the downside in dollar Yen
claims.claim: If the Bank of Japan loosens its yield-curve band while dollar-yen is stretched near 146, there is large downside risk in USDJPY (a policy-change catalyst), whereas long dollar has paid so far.
claims.indicator: BoJ yield band (0.25% upper); USDJPY level
claims.direction: short USDJPY on band release; long USD until then
claims.conditions: depends on BoJ abandoning the band

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: markets were less efficient then and so when markets are inefficient there's a lot more to do and there tend to be overshoots and different uh you know uh Market momentum events
claims.claim: Macro was better in the 80s and 90s because markets were less efficient, producing more overshoots and momentum events; the efficient low-inflation 2010s left little to harvest.
claims.conditions: low-inflation, efficient-market regimes reduce macro opportunity

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: macro became an unpopular strategy it wasn't doing particularly well on the whole in that sort of post-gfc decade
claims.claim: Macro hedge funds were unpopular and weak post-GFC because inflation near zero and policy on hold made beta-heavy portfolios win.
claims.conditions: zero inflation and on-hold central banks hurt macro
claims.testable: partly - fund index returns by regime

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: we generally generated positive returns so it didn't cost you money to be more Diversified and when you need that diversity in a year like this we're providing it
claims.claim: Macro funds delivered positive returns even in the weak decade and diversification when needed in 2022, so allocating to them was not costly.
claims.indicator: macro fund return correlation to equities/bonds

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: if you go back to the volkier it was really really tricky to get rid of inflation it took a very very long time it did not happen in two years
claims.claim: Volcker-era analogy: disinflation took far longer than two years and the central bank eased too early and had to hike again, so inflation is sticky and hard for the Fed to manage.
claims.direction: inflation stays above target for years; bonds unattractive

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: some of them are out of their purview the supply chain disruption the FED really can't manage that right and so the FED really can't manage what energy prices are
claims.claim: Supply-chain and energy-price driven inflation is outside Fed control, so rate hikes cannot fully remove it.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: I think the Market's expecting the FED to be able to start easing at the end of 2023 I'm skeptical
claims.claim: View: market pricing of Fed easing by end-2023 is too early; inflation falls in 2023 but is not near 2% until 2025 if then.
claims.indicator: Fed funds futures vs realised inflation
claims.direction: fade pricing of cuts in 2023; stay short duration

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: I think we want to err on the side of getting it comfortably down to Target it's going to be uh painful from for the economy Powell's conceded that
claims.claim: Credibility camp view: the Fed must over-tighten to re-anchor expectations, implying a recession whose timing and length are the open questions.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: inflation Genie got out of the bag it's hard to put it back in it's kind of like an ocean liner it takes a while for it to turn around
claims.claim: Inflation has momentum: once expectations and wage dynamics shift, disinflation is slow.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: you've got uh inflation in the Netherlands I believe it's 15 uh you've got the cost of power in Europe
claims.claim: European inflation is very high and supply-side driven by power costs, while US inflation is partly supply and partly labour-driven, which widens central bank divergence.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: there is a complacency that has developed in the workforce where the expectation about constantly higher compensation and so on and firms competing for precious few employees have been you know contributing to inflation
claims.claim: Wage-price pressure from tight labour markets and employee expectations that have never seen a recession keep US inflation elevated and will reverse only slowly.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: corrodis tournaments up I think in April of uh 23 so that's going to be an important uh Catalyst to watch do they loosen that band
claims.claim: BoJ governor transition in April 2023 is a catalyst for loosening yield curve control, triggering a yen reaction (intervention already signals discomfort with weakness).

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: we may be in a trading range for equities for some number of years
claims.claim: After 12 years of straight-up equities a more normal two-way market and a multi-year trading range is expected.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: I think it will be hotter for a while uh I think that's a I I don't disagree with the goal of having two percent inflation
claims.claim: Inflation will run above the 2% target for a while despite the target being worthy.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: for all of the years I've been in finance most of them there were something called duration risk for being in longer dated bonds and that's completely missing at the moment
claims.claim: Term premium is missing in long bonds; with inflation lasting several years, 10-year yields at 3.95% are mispriced and should be 50-100bp higher, with the curve re-steepening.
claims.conditions: if inflation persists three to five years

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: we want to be able to exit positions without a great deal of expense and that's a Paramount uh you know importance to me
claims.claim: Risk approach: trade mostly very liquid markets, with daily risk committee, so positions can be exited cheaply and early rather than late at greater expense.
claims.testable: partly - liquidity constraint testable in backtests

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: it's been a great year to trade foreign exchange you know there's been a huge move in dollar euro dollar euro was 120 now it's you know 97 or something
claims.claim: 2022 FX trends (EURUSD 1.20 to 0.97, USDJPY higher, sterling down) were the best macro trades, consistent with rate divergence.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: income we've done quite well uh you know being short bonds of various durations and various different uh geographies
claims.claim: Short bonds across durations and regions plus energy and long dollar were profitable in 2022, as rates rose with inflation.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: the dollar has been at profitable trade it's a crowded trade too do you think it has more room to run yeah it's definitely expensive
claims.claim: Long dollar is crowded and expensive, so the manager keeps only light exposure and expects only a little more upside.
claims.testable: partly - positioning data (CFTC) could be tested

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: our quantitative systems are somewhat longer term in nature they would tend to move around say over a period of weeks and months whereas our discretionary Traders they move very quickly
claims.claim: Two-layer structure: quant systems hold positions weeks to months while discretionary traders flip within days, staying open-minded to price information.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: one of the reasons I'm concerned about inflation being around for uh you know a longer period Than People expect is our energy policies are green
claims.claim: Underinvestment in conventional energy during the green transition plus OPEC supply cuts keeps energy (crude in the 90s) and headline inflation high, especially in Europe.
claims.indicator: crude oil price; energy supply policy

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: we try and stay away from things that we really don't have an engine for
claims.claim: Discipline: keep crypto positions very small and avoid markets where the firm has no edge or process.

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: if there was ever a year people wanted gold to perform and uh you know be an inflation hedge it's down
claims.claim: Gold failed as an inflation hedge in 2022, falling 10-15% while inflation spiked; speaker does not know why, but quant models were short.
claims.direction: gold did not hedge inflation; short gold

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: the two-year is sort of pricing in 4-3 now for uh 75 at year end uh and then I think we start to see that ease back down in the middle of 23 to maybe four and a quarter
claims.claim: View (Oct 2022): the front end prices a policy peak near 4.75% by year-end easing to about 4.25% by mid-2023, while the 10-year sits at 3.95%, leaving the curve inverted; he sees the long end, not the front end, as mispriced.
claims.indicator: 2-year Treasury / priced policy path vs 10-year yield
claims.direction: front end peaks then eases; 10-year too low
claims.testable: yes - compare priced path with realised policy rates

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: Rachel rates have moved a lot but they needed to and I think they'll keep moving
claims.claim: Real rates have risen a lot, as was necessary, and will keep rising, which supports further bond weakness.
claims.testable: yes - subsequent change in TIPS real yields

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: I think it's already made a big move so I don't know how much weaker it really gets uh you know I so I would be kind of neutral at these levels personally
claims.claim: After sterling's large fall (bottom near 1.035), he is neutral: once a trend has already made a big move he sees little remaining edge in pressing it.
claims.testable: partly - returns after extreme multi-month currency moves

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: the policy priority was really bringing inflation that had been too low for the past decade back up to Target and that very low inflation backdrop had allowed the FED to be quick to ease and slow to tighten
claims.claim: Pre-pandemic, persistently low inflation let the Fed ease quickly and tighten slowly (2015-18 hikes every other meeting at 25bp), creating the fed put and well-telegraphed policy.
claims.testable: partly - reaction function can be estimated by regime

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: the Fed was very confident at that time calling in high inflation transitory because for so long inflation had been so low
claims.claim: The Fed's new average inflation targeting framework (Aug 2020) and its 'transitory' call made it slow to respond to inflation, producing a lag between inflation data and policy that a researcher can exploit.
claims.indicator: Fed policy rate vs inflation prints
claims.direction: Fed behind the curve; short bonds, long USD
claims.conditions: after a long low-inflation period when the Fed is anchored to old regime
claims.testable: partly - lag of Fed vs Taylor-rule gap testable

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we could come into the Year and have a strong view about where inflation was going where the labor market was going and see that the Fed was really wrongly positioned for this environment
claims.claim: Edge arises when economic research shows the central bank is mispositioned relative to inflation and labour data, since previously telegraphed policy had left little room for such an edge.
claims.indicator: inflation and labour market data vs central bank positioning
claims.testable: partly - compare Taylor-rule gap with market pricing

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: one of the things that I think was so different for Central Bank watching
claims.claim: Central banks worldwide surprised on how aggressive they would be (e.g. 75bp hikes) after a year earlier still doing QE, so the policy debate shifted from taper to pace of tightening.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: my team doesn't have a house view that PMS have to put on
claims.claim: Process: the economist team provides research and flags where Fed thinking differs from consensus, but portfolio managers express it independently.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: that they might for example be considering running off their balance
claims.claim: Example of early reading of Fed communications (Dec 2021 press conference hints at earlier balance sheet runoff while still doing QE) as an opportunity outside consensus.
claims.indicator: Fed press conference language; balance sheet runoff timing
claims.direction: short bonds ahead of earlier balance sheet runoff
claims.conditions: when market consensus is not pricing it
claims.testable: partly - text analysis of FOMC communication

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: I think anyone working right now unless they're been working a really long time has never seen inflation like this and when I got into business in the mid 90s used to say inflation was the hardest variable to predict
claims.claim: Inflation is the hardest variable to predict and models built on 20 years of 0.2% monthly prints break down, so central bank response models are unreliable.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: Global central banks that hike in response to a high headline CPI or even you know the FED height texture in response to a higher than expected Universe University of Michigan uh um inflation expectations survey
claims.claim: Central banks now react to headline CPI and even the Michigan inflation expectations survey, so those releases are tradable policy triggers.
claims.indicator: headline CPI; University of Michigan inflation expectations

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: you have governments that what are they doing they're actually spending more money to help people afford higher prices
claims.claim: Fiscal support for higher prices works against monetary tightening (Back to the Future dynamic), sustaining inflation.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: the negative correlation between stocks and bonds a lot of people to construct um such uh positive expected value portfolios that's gone
claims.claim: The negative stock-bond correlation underpinning 60/40 portfolios has gone in the inflation regime, so diversification between them fails.
claims.conditions: when inflation is high and central banks hike
claims.testable: yes - rolling stock-bond correlation vs inflation

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: a reversal of the globalization that we've seen for most of our careers um I think a reversal of the capital versus labor Dynamics where labor is developed more power again
claims.claim: Secular changes - deglobalisation and labour regaining power vs capital - support structurally higher inflation.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: it puts a real premium on maybe risk proper risk management
claims.claim: In a regime where economists and traders are on equal footing with no precedent, premium is on common sense, imagination and risk management.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: so it's set up risk parity for for decades
claims.claim: Risk parity worked for decades on falling rates and QE tamped volatility, peaking when $7 trillion of debt was negative-yielding and equity valuations at highs; it has since been thrown out.
claims.indicator: risk parity returns; negative-yielding debt stock
claims.conditions: falling-rate low-vol regime; fails when stocks and bonds fall together
claims.testable: yes - risk parity backtest by regime

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: QE brings down Vol and it and it um you know allows people to kind of go well they want the central banks want you to go further out in the risk Spectrum
claims.claim: QE suppresses volatility and pushes investors out the risk spectrum (3% mortgages, cheap credit), whereas withdrawing it raises volatility.
claims.testable: yes - volatility vs balance sheet change

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: there is a fed put but it's it struck so far down that we're not quite sure where that is yet
claims.claim: The Fed put still exists but its strike is far lower because inflation limits easing; buying dips on pivot hopes is the old playbook.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: the adage is no one makes money in a bear Market because the bear Market rallies are so vicious
claims.claim: Bear markets contain vicious rallies (summer 2022 stocks +20%, 10-year notes rallying 75bp), so a trend-following short must manage sentiment-driven snapbacks.
claims.testable: yes - rally size in bear markets

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: short risk parody which meaning short stocks and short bonds Dollar's been very strong
claims.claim: Most 2022 returns came from short stocks plus short bonds (anti-risk-parity) and long dollar, with extra gains in yen and the Mexican peso (reshoring flows despite carry).
claims.direction: short stocks, short bonds, long USD

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: this idea of matching conviction two positions and trading dynamically
claims.claim: Macro value comes from scaling positions to conviction, which creates risk-management challenges.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: in times of the higher correlation we actually have a higher information ratio among our PMS however they also tend to be times of higher volatility
claims.claim: When themes are clear, PM returns correlate more and information ratio is higher, but volatility is higher so position sizes shrink, offsetting risk.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: tail risks tend to be higher because people have higher position sizes to offset the fact that volatility is low
claims.claim: Low-vol periods give low VaR but larger tail risk because positions are sized up; in high-vol 2022 VaR is high but tails smaller.
claims.testable: yes - tail loss vs vol regime

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: it makes statistics like stress tests more valuable because really that's what we're concerned about in markets like this where Gap risk is really what you need to be concerned about
claims.claim: With unstable correlations VaR loses value; stress tests and gap-risk analysis matter more.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: the fact that's going down to two is is ludicrous
claims.claim: View: inflation will stay high (or possibly go to deflation) rather than return smoothly to 2%, because the target is arbitrary; liquidity tightening globally is bad for risk assets.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we think inflation will mean persistently High
claims.claim: Entrenched services and core goods inflation means the Fed will lift the terminal rate to 4% then 5% and soft landing odds are low.
claims.indicator: core goods and services inflation; terminal rate

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: we're seeing those central banks having to tighten into recessions
claims.claim: European central banks face energy-driven inflation and second-round effects yet must tighten into recession, reversing the fed-put logic of accommodating downside growth risk.

claims.speaker: Katie Woodridge
claims.quote: there will be really interesting opportunities as perhaps central banks move to easing Cycles
claims.claim: If inflation unexpectedly cooled, easing cycles would also be an opportunity; the team holds both scenarios.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: defies the imagination that Japan is going to be the only developed country on Earth that doesn't have inflation
claims.claim: Japan's inflation (30-year high at 3%), YCC testing, weak yen and intervention limits create trade opportunities, with BoJ leadership change due.
claims.direction: long inflation in Japan; USDJPY risk
claims.conditions: BoJ must buy JGBs while defending yen

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: the big variable in Europe is is the winner I mean if it's a cold winter
claims.claim: Key variables: European winter weather, China zero-covid policy after party congress.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: does do real yields keep going because we're uh shrinking our balance sheet larger than we really ever have
claims.claim: Quantitative tightening raises real yields until yields get so high central banks might flinch.
claims.conditions: yields high enough to stress markets

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: they've survived in the markets for a long period of time because they know how to size their positions for for the long run
claims.claim: Risk management structure: frontline PM sizing, a daily risk committee (4000 meetings since GFC), risk team running Greeks, hundreds of shocks and dozens of stress tests, plus qualitative 'why' from the trading floor.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: I don't say controlling with necessarily the portfolio managers are controlling the risk and we're just advising them
claims.claim: Risk team advises and monitors; PMs own risk, with committee as cold-eyes review.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: you size or positions and ball units so and and Chris said this earlier you know and higher it falls higher your emotional size is smaller
claims.claim: Size positions in volatility units so higher volatility means smaller positions; prepare for tails and gap risk.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: liquidity in the markets are terrible and so some trades you just might not take
claims.claim: Poor liquidity means some trades cannot be sized, so illiquid ideas are skipped; place a premium on liquid instruments.

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: there is a factor that's I would call a sentiment Factor so sometimes things get correlated everything that's overbought gets sold and everything that's open
claims.claim: A sentiment factor: everything overbought gets sold and oversold gets bought, correlating positions; PMs monitor this.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: these things will all be one trade so the idea of shrinking the book
claims.claim: Across asset classes dollar, rates and equities become one trade into central bank meetings, so book size is shrunk to avoid a triple-sized bet.
claims.conditions: correlations near one around central bank meetings

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: there's investing in trading and you can do both so you have your themes your have your core views
claims.claim: Combine core thematic positions with trading around them (add on retraces, press squeezes, fade, take profits at key levels).

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: what positions are too big and what positions are too small
claims.claim: Daily team risk meeting asks which positions are too big or too small.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: portfolio managers especially this year where there are a lot of opportunities to react have been tending to scale down into events and then reacting to what happens
claims.claim: With no edge on any given event, scale down into events and react afterwards, using liquidity to rescale (unlike long-only or illiquid books).

claims.speaker: Pablo Calderini
claims.quote: I think it's time that we start seeing the 2010-20 period as an anomaly
claims.claim: Pre-2010 volatility was the norm; the 2010-20 suppressed-vol era (easing met every shock) was an anomaly, so expect higher volatility ahead and inflation requires tighter policy responses.

claims.speaker: Chris McCann
claims.quote: when we're doing asset allocation every month we're trying to make sure that we're taking pairwise correlation into account so that we're not putting all of our assets into one style of investing
claims.claim: Capital is allocated across portfolio managers monthly using their pairwise return correlations, and PMs are hired for what they add that is different, so the book is not concentrated in one style.
claims.testable: yes - diversification ratio of correlation-aware vs naive allocation

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: at what point can they really step in and intervene in the currency if they're um you know buying all the treasuries or all the jgbs
claims.claim: Japan's yield-curve control (buying large amounts of JGBs) conflicts with intervening to support the yen, so with inflation at a 30-year high and markets testing YCC, the policy mix looks unsustainable and is a trade opportunity.
claims.indicator: BoJ yield-curve control, JGB purchases, USDJPY intervention
claims.conditions: Japanese inflation rising while YCC holds
claims.testable: partly - yen and JGB moves around intervention and YCC changes

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: the central banks going probably a little farther than the market
claims.claim: View: central banks will tighten somewhat further than market pricing implies because inflation is sticky.
claims.testable: yes - realised vs priced terminal rate

claims.speaker: Peter Chapson
claims.quote: for me it's bottom up so I try to find ideas um and once so the ideas come together and I look at my overall risk and make sure it's oriented to um the way we want it
claims.claim: Portfolio construction method: generate trade ideas bottom-up, then check the combined book's overall risk orientation, using the same process in quiet (2018) and busy (2022) years.

claims.speaker: David Keelan
claims.quote: if you write it it works you feel it it's at the portfolio level but you don't want to be too big that if there's some noise you get shaken out
claims.claim: Sizing rule: a position should be big enough to matter at the portfolio level if right, but small enough that ordinary noise does not force you out; getting the theme right matters more than structure.
claims.testable: partly - stop-out frequency vs position size in volatility units

claims.speaker: Ken Tropin
claims.quote: in 1998 in an effort to diversify the sources of alpha that Graham is able to take advantage of we began to build a discretionary business
